posts.hook: Here is what a Home Safety Check actually covers — and what it doesn't.

posts.hook: What does a full rewire actually involve, day by day?
posts.body:
Most people imagine a rewire means living on a building site for a month. It's the main reason people put it off.

Here is what it actually looks like on a typical 1930s semi:

Day 1: First fix. Cables run through the house. Boards up in places, yes, but contained to specific areas.

Days 2–4: Continuing the first fix room by room, working methodically. You're still living in the house.

Day 5: Second fix. Sockets, switches, lights all fitted. Fuse board installed.

Day 6: Testing, certification, tidy-up. House gets hoovered.

Six days. Not a month. The house doesn't get left in pieces at the end of each day.

posts.hook: Five things that tell you your old fuse board needs replacing — not next year, now.
posts.body:
Slide 1: It has old-style rewirable fuses — the ceramic ones with wire threaded through them. These trip by melting. That's not a safety feature.

Slide 2: There's no RCD protection. An RCD cuts the power in a fraction of a second if there's a fault. Without one, it doesn't.

Slide 3: The circuits aren't labelled. That's not just inconvenient — it means the last person in there either didn't check, or didn't care.

Slide 4: The casing is cracked, discoloured, or has been repaired with tape. These things are supposed to be sealed.

Slide 5: You've added sockets, a new shower, a dishwasher — and nobody has checked the board since. The load may have changed. The protection hasn't.

If any of these match your house, it's worth getting it looked at. Dan will photograph everything and tell you in plain English exactly what's there.

posts.hook: What it looks like when we open up a fuse board that hasn't been touched in 20 years.
posts.body:
It's usually a few things at once.

Old rewirable fuses, sometimes replaced with fuses of the wrong rating — which is worse than leaving them as they were. Wiring from two or three different decades, sometimes three different colours because the standards changed and whoever worked on it last didn't worry about that. Circuits running to parts of the house that weren't on the original plan because someone added a socket extension at some point.

Sometimes there's a label that says 'kitchen' and goes to the bathroom.

None of it is unusual in a 1930s or 1950s semi that's changed hands a few times. It just means there's a real job to do.

Dan photographs all of it before writing anything up. That's where the fixed price comes from — the actual job, not a guess.
